title: Mockery in place of argument
source_text: Εἶθ᾿ ἑξῆς ἐπαναλαμβάνει πολλάκις ἤδη εἰπὼν τὰ περὶ τῆς γνώμης Μαρκίωνος, καὶ πῇ μὲν ἀληθῶς τὰ Μαρκίωνος ἐκτίθεται πῇ δὲ κἀκείνων παρήκουσεν· πρὸς ἣν οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἡμᾶς ἀπαντᾶν ἢ καὶ ἐλέγχειν. εἶτα πάλιν ἑαυτῷ ἐπιφέρει τὰ ὑπὲρ Μαρκίωνος καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ λέγων, τίνα μὲν ἐκφεύγουσι τῶν ἐγκλημάτων τίσι δὲ περιπίπτουσι· καὶ ὅτε βούλεται συναγορεύειν τῷ φάσκοντι λόγῳ πεπροφητεῦσθαι αὐτὸν, ἵνα κατηγορήσῃ Μαρκίωνος καὶ τῶν ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ. σαφῶς φησιν ὅτι πόθεν ἀποδειχθήσεται θεοῦ παῖς ὁ τοιαῦτα κολασθεὶς. εἰ μὴ περὶ τούτου προείρηται; εἶτα πάλιν παίζει καὶ, ὡς ἔθος αὐτῷ, χλευάζει δύο εἰσάγων υἱοὺς θεῶν, τοῦ δημιουργοῦ ἕνα καὶ τοῦ κατὰ Μαρκίωνα θεοῦ ἕτερον, καὶ ἀναζωγραφεῖ αὐτῶν μονομαχίας, λέγων αὐτὰς εἶναι ὡς τῶν ὀρτύγων, καὶ τῶν πατέρων θεομαχίας· ἢ διὰ γῆρας ἀχρήστους αὐτοὺς ὄντας καὶ ληροῦντας μηδὲν μὲν ἀλλήλους διατιθέναι, ἐᾶν δὲ τοὺς παῖδας μάχεσθαι. ὅπερ οὖν εἶπεν ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω, τοῦτο φήσομεν πρὸς αὐτόν· ποία γραῦς καταβαυκαλῶσα παιδίον οὐκ αἰδεσθήσεται τοιαῦτα λέγειν, ὁποῖα οὗτος ἐν τῷ ἐπιγραφομένῳ ἀληθεῖ λόγῳ; δέον γὰρ αὐτὸν πραγματικῶς στῆναι πρὸς τοὺς λόγους, ὁ δὲ ἐάσας τὰ πράγματα παίζει καὶ βωμολοχεῖ οἰόμενος μίμους γράφειν ἤ τινα σκώμματα, οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι ἡ τοιαύτη ἀγωγὴ τῶν λόγων παρὰ τὴν πρόθεσιν τὴν αὐτοῦ ἐστι, βουλομένου καταλιπόντας ἡμᾶς χριστιανισμὸν προσέχειν αὐτοῦ τοῖς δόγμασιν· ἅτινα εἰ μὲν ἐσεμνολόγει, τάχα πιθανώτερα ἦν· ἐπεὶ δὲ χλευάζει καὶ παίζει καὶ βωμολοχεῖ, φήσομεν ὅτι ἀπορίᾳ σεμνῶν λόγων (οὐ γὰρ εἶχεν αὐτοὺς οὐδὲ ἠπίστατο) εἰς τοσαύτην ἐνέπεσε φλυαρίαν.
pass_a_gloss: Then next he takes up again (ἐπαναλαμβάνει), having already said many times, the things about the opinion (γνώμη) of Marcion; and in part he sets out (ἐκτίθεται) Marcion's views truly (ἀληθῶς), in part he misheard (παρήκουσεν) even those; to which (opinion) it is not necessary (ἀναγκαῖον) for us to reply (ἀπαντᾶν) or even refute (ἐλέγχειν). Then again he brings against/up for himself (ἑαυτῷ ἐπιφέρει) the things for Marcion and against him, saying which of the charges (ἐγκλήματα) they escape (ἐκφεύγουσι) and into which they fall (περιπίπτουσι); and when he wishes to plead alongside (συναγορεύειν) the argument (λόγος) claiming that he had been prophesied (πεπροφητεῦσθαι), in order to accuse (κατηγορήσῃ) Marcion and those from him, he says clearly: 'From where will he be shown (ἀποδειχθήσεται) a child of God (θεοῦ παῖς), the one punished (κολασθείς) in such ways, if it was not foretold (προείρηται) about him?' Then again he plays (παίζει) and, as is his custom (ἔθος), mocks (χλευάζει), introducing two sons of gods (υἱοὺς θεῶν), one of the craftsman (δημιουργός) and another of the god according to Marcion, and paints (ἀναζωγραφεῖ) their single combats (μονομαχίας), saying they are as those of quails (ὀρτύγων), and the god-battles (θεομαχίας) of the fathers; or that through old age (γῆρας) being useless (ἀχρήστους) and talking nonsense (ληροῦντας) they do nothing to each other but let (ἐᾶν) the children fight. What then he said in the earlier parts, this we shall say to him: what old woman (γραῦς) lulling to sleep (καταβαυκαλῶσα) a child would not be ashamed (αἰδεσθήσεται) to say such things as he in the [book] entitled True Word/Doctrine (ἀληθὴς λόγος)? For it being needful for him to stand (στῆναι) in earnest/on the facts (πραγματικῶς) against the arguments, he, letting the facts (πράγματα) go, plays and acts the buffoon (βωμολοχεῖ), thinking to write mimes (μίμους) or some jibes (σκώμματα), not seeing that such conduct (ἀγωγή) of the arguments is contrary to his own purpose (πρόθεσις), wishing us, having abandoned Christianity (χριστιανισμός), to attend to his doctrines (δόγμασιν); which, if he spoke with solemnity (ἐσεμνολόγει), would perhaps have been more persuasive (πιθανώτερα); but since he mocks and plays and buffoons, we shall say that through lack (ἀπορία) of dignified arguments (σεμνῶν λόγων) (for he neither had them nor understood them) he fell into such great babble (φλυαρία).
pass_b_english: Next he goes back over what he has often said before about Marcion’s opinion. In some places he sets out Marcion’s views truly; in others he has misheard even those. We need not answer that opinion, or even refute it.

Then he again brings up, on his own account, what can be said for Marcion and what against him, saying which charges they escape and into which they fall. And when he wants to side with the argument that claims Jesus was foretold, so as to accuse Marcion and his followers, he says plainly: “How will one who was punished like this be shown to be a child of God, unless it has been foretold about him?”

Then he jests again and, as is his habit, mocks, bringing in two sons of gods, one the son of the Creator and the other the son of Marcion’s god. He paints a picture of their single combats, saying they are like the fights of quails, and of the battles of their fathers, the gods; or else he says that the fathers, useless and doting from old age, do nothing to one another but leave their sons to fight.

So what he himself said earlier, we shall say to him: what old woman lulling a child to sleep would not be ashamed to say such things as he says in his book entitled The True Doctrine? For he ought to have stood up to the arguments in earnest; instead he leaves the substance aside and jests and plays the buffoon, thinking that he is writing mimes or lampoons. He does not see that such a way of conducting the argument works against his own purpose, since he wants us to leave Christianity and attend to his doctrines. Had he set these out with dignity, they might perhaps have been more persuasive; but since he mocks and jests and plays the buffoon, we shall say that it was for lack of serious arguments (for he neither had them nor knew any) that he fell into such great nonsense.

choices.choice: Origen turns back on Celsus his own earlier taunt (the old woman lulling a child to sleep), which Celsus had used against the Christians earlier in Book 6 (about 6.34); left uncited inline as it is not Scripture. πρὸς ἣν refers to γνώμη (Marcion’s opinion). θεοῦ παῖς rendered ‘a child of God’ to keep παῖς distinct from υἱός; it sits inside Celsus’s words, so lower-case ‘child’. ‘Sons of gods’, ‘Marcion’s god’ and ‘the gods’ stay lower case: this is Celsus’s mocking frame, and Marcion’s second god is not God for Origen; ‘the Creator’ (δημιουργός) is capitalised because Origen takes him to be God. The quail line and the ‘useless from old age’ line are indirect report in the Greek (infinitives/participles), so they are not put in quotation marks. ἐπιγραφομένῳ ἀληθεῖ λόγῳ rendered with the house title The True Doctrine.
προείρηται tense: 'unless this had been foretold' -> 'unless it has been foretold' (perfect; 'this' was added)
ἐπιγραφομένῳ: 'the book he entitled' -> 'his book entitled' (no added agency)
restored γάρ: 'For he ought to have stood up to the arguments'
